papers.title: Comparative effects of six exercise modalities on global cognitive function in Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and mild cognitive impairment: a systematic review and network meta-analysis.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Alzheimer's disease (AD), Parkinson's disease (PD), and mild cognitive impairment (MCI) are commonly accompanied by cognitive decline. Although exercise is recommended as a non-pharmacological strategy, the comparative effects of different exercise modalities on global cognition remain uncertain. OBJECTIVE: To compare six exercise modalities-aerobic exercise (AE), mind-body exercise (MBE), resistance training (RT), multi-component exercise (MCE), flexibility training (FT), and functional training (FTr)-for global cognitive function in people with AD, PD, or MCI, and to explore dose-related associations. METHODS: PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Library, and Web of Science were searched from inception to January 26, 2026. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were synthesized using a frequentist random-effects network meta-analysis (NMA) with standardized mean differences (SMDs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Treatment rankings were summarized using SUCRA. Subgroup analyses, meta-regression, diagnosis-related sensitivity analyses, and CINeMA certainty assessments were also performed. RESULTS: Twenty-eight trials involving 1,993 participants were included. Compared with control group (CG), AE [SMD = 0.47, 95% CI (0.18, 0.77)], MBE [SMD = 0.79, 95% CI (0.46, 1.11)], RT [SMD = 1.50, 95% CI (0.77, 2.23)], MCE [SMD = 0.83, 95% CI (0.26, 1.40)], and FTr [SMD = 0.83, 95% CI (0.13, 1.53)] improved global cognition, whereas FT showed no clear effect [SMD = -0.20, 95% CI (-1.27,0.87)]. RT showed the largest effect estimate and the most favorable ranking. However, substantial heterogeneity and sparse evidence for several modalities limit firm conclusions. papers.title: Exercise modality and planned weekly exercise exposure for motor outcomes in Parkinson's disease: a systematic review, Bayesian network meta-analysis, and meta-regression.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Exercise modality and planned weekly structured-exercise exposure may provide complementary information for Parkinson's disease motor outcomes, but their outcome-specific effects and evidential confidence remain uncertain. METHODS: We synthesized 173 randomized trials using covariance-aware Bayesian random-effects network meta-analysis for motor symptoms, balance, walking speed, and Timed Up and Go (TUG). A key secondary analysis estimated exercise-class-adjusted associations per 250 metabolic equivalent task minutes/week, with pre-specified sensitivity analyses. RESULTS: The category NMA networks included 110, 106, 89, and 96 trials for Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale part III (UPDRS III), balance, walking speed, and TUG, respectively. Mind-body exercise had the largest posterior median versus non-exercise control for UPDRS III (g = 0.65, 95% credible interval [CrI] 0.42-0.87). In the reconstructed, exercise-category-adjusted dose models, planned weekly structured-exercise exposure was positively associated at the trial level with UPDRS III (0.121 SMD per + 250 MET-min/week, 95% CrI 0.055-0.194), balance (0.111, 0.047-0.184), and TUG (0.124, 0.058-0.190), but not walking speed (0.008, - 0.063 to 0.076). The TUG estimate attenuated after P95 dose truncation. All active-versus-control prediction intervals crossed zero; CINeMA confidence was low or very low. The evidence did not establish a universally best modality, an optimal dose, or an individual causal target. Higher planned weekly exposure was associated at the trial level with greater average improvement in UPDRS III, balance, and TUG, whereas walking speed showed no clear association. However, within-class randomized dose-contrast estimates were imprecise for all four outcomes, and the TUG association was sensitive to the high-dose tail.

papers.title: Consensus-based perspectives on integrating IPX203 into Parkinson's disease management.
papers.abstract: Motor fluctuations are a common and burdensome complication of Parkinson's disease (PD) when the disease progresses, largely driven by the short half-life and variable absorption of immediate-release (IR) levodopa. IPX203 is a next-generation modified-release levodopa/carbidopa formulation that delivers rapid onset and sustained plasma levodopa concentrations through IR granules and extended-release pellets. Clinical studies have shown that IPX203 increases Good ON time (ON time without dyskinesia plus ON time with non-troublesome dyskinesia, equivalent to ON time without troublesome dyskinesia), reduces OFF time and improves motor symptom control compared with IR levodopa/carbidopa. In anticipation of the introduction of IPX203 in Europe, nine PD specialists convened to develop consensus recommendations for its use in clinical practice. Through a structured process incorporating predefined statements, voting and moderated discussion, the group reached high levels of agreement (88.9% to 100%) across seven topics. These included defining motor symptoms control, identifying patients most likely to benefit from IPX203, positioning of IPX203 within the treatment pathway, practical considerations for switching to IPX203 from current regimens and recommendations for monitoring and follow-up. The experts emphasised that IPX203 should be considered for patients with motor fluctuations insufficiently controlled on optimised oral levodopa therapy, before introduction of device-aided therapies. They highlighted the need for flexible dose adjustments, comprehensive patient and neurologist education and practical tools to support conversion to IPX203. This consensus insight provides practical guidance for integrating IPX203 into routine care of PD patients with motor fluctuations, aiming to increase mobility and reduce treatment burden for patients with PD.

papers.title: Cerebellar Network Organization in Parkinson's Disease: Functional Connectivity across Motor and Cognitive Circuits.
papers.journal: Movement disorders : official journal of the Movement Disorder Society
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: The cerebellum is increasingly recognized as a key contributor to cognitive reserve and network organization in Parkinson's disease (PD). However, the relationship of cerebello-cortical and cerebello-basal ganglia connectivity with cognitive status and nigrostriatal integrity remains incompletely understood. METHODS: Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data from 172 participants with PD in the Parkinson's Precision Medicine Initiative were analyzed. Cerebello-basal ganglia and cerebello-cortical connectivity were investigated using region of interest (ROI)-to-ROI and seed-to-voxel approaches. Cerebellar connectivity was examined in relation to cognitive status, age, disease duration, motor severity, dopaminergic medication exposure, and contralateral putaminal striatal binding ratio (SBR). RESULTS: PD participants demonstrated robust positive cerebello-basal ganglia connectivity, particularly between lobule VI/vermis VI and the pallidum. Greater age was associated with widespread reductions in cerebello-basal ganglia coupling. Longer disease duration was associated with stronger connectivity within cerebellar and basal ganglia circuits, and among cognitively unimpaired participants, stronger lobule V connectivity with temporal regions. After adjustment for contralateral putaminal SBR, cognitively unimpaired participants generally demonstrated greater connectivity between left cerebellar regions and frontal networks, whereas cognitively impaired participants showed greater connectivity from posterior cerebellar and vermal regions, including regions implicated in cognitive processing, to temporal, parahippocampal, occipital, parietal, and somatosensory regions. CONCLUSIONS: Cerebellar functional connectivity in PD shows region-specific differences across cognitive status rather than uniform network loss with cognitive impairment. papers.title: Tau protein in Parkinson's disease: advances in phosphoproteomics and molecular dynamics simulations.
papers.abstract: Tau dysregulation, particularly abnormal phosphorylation, is increasingly implicated in Parkinson's disease (PD) and in the pathogenic interaction between Tau and α-synuclein. This review proposes an integrated PD-focused workflow connecting phosphoproteomic discovery, structural modeling, computational drug discovery, and experimental validation. Phosphoproteomic analyses of post-mortem brain tissue, biofluids, and patient-derived dopaminergic neuronal models can identify candidate Tau phosphosignatures associated with vulnerable brain regions, α-synuclein pathology, genetic background, or clinical progression. Molecular dynamics simulations can then evaluate how these signatures alter Tau conformation, microtubule binding, aggregation-prone motifs, membrane association, and pathogenic protein interactions. The resulting structural information can guide ensemble docking, chemoinformatics, and artificial intelligence approaches to prioritize conformer-selective ligands and regulatory targets. Candidate biomarkers should subsequently be validated in independent and longitudinal PD cohorts, whereas therapeutic candidates require mechanistic and functional validation in PD-relevant experimental models before clinical translation. This iterative framework may help distinguish mechanistically relevant Tau phosphoconformers from nonspecific phosphorylation changes, support biomarker-based patient stratification, and focus therapeutic development on structurally defined pathological states. Because much of the available structural evidence derives from Alzheimer's disease and other tauopathies, direct validation in PD remains essential. By linking PD-derived and disease-relevant molecular evidence with atomistic mechanisms and therapeutic prioritization, this workflow may support biomarker-informed strategies aimed at restoring Tau homeostasis and disrupting pathogenic Tau-α-synuclein interactions.

papers.title: Non-motor correlates of anxiety in de novo Parkinson's disease: a cross-sectional study with exploratory subgroup analyses.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Anxiety is a prevalent early non-motor symptom of Parkinson's disease (PD), but its clinical correlates remain poorly defined in de novo METHODS: Anxiety was assessed with the Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale; multivariate logistic regression and prespecified stratified analyses by age, sex, disease duration, Hoehn-Yahr stage and motor severity were performed. RESULTS: Clinically significant anxiety was detected in 44.0% of PD patients versus 8.1% of controls (p CONCLUSION: These findings indicate that non-motor abnormalities, rather than motor impairment, are associated with anxiety in early PD after adjustment for demographic and motor covariates. The distinct correlative patterns across subgroups provide preliminary clinical clues for the heterogeneous neurodegenerative processes underlying PD-related anxiety, and support routine screening of depressive, sleep and olfactory symptoms to facilitate anxiety risk stratification at initial diagnosis.

papers.title: Incidental Finding of an Asymptomatic Perielectrode Cyst After Deep Brain Stimulation for Parkinson's Disease.
papers.abstract: Implanted intracerebral devices can lead to infection, hemorrhage, or the formation of fluid-filled cysts. Formation of a perielectrode cyst after deep brain stimulation (DBS) has been reported in a limited number of patients. Additionally, diverse causes and clinical presentations have been associated with these cysts. We present a case of perielectrode cyst formation three months after implantation of a subthalamic nucleus DBS (STN-DBS) for Parkinson's disease (PD). A 59-year-old woman was diagnosed with PD in 2011. In November 2023, the patient underwent staged placement of an STN-DBS without perioperative complications. Immediate postoperative cerebral CT ruled out acute complications. Postoperatively, the patient showed clear clinical improvement, and a substantial reduction in the levodopa dose was achieved (1,500 mg/24 h vs. 250 mg/24 h). There was a significant change in neurocognitive testing three months postoperatively, with a decrease in the Montreal Cognitive Assessment score from 29/30 to 24/30. Follow-up cerebral MRI showed a perielectrode cystic lesion around the left electrode. The patient's clinical status and electrode impedances remained unchanged during follow-up. Serial imaging demonstrated gradual regression of the cyst. Perielectrode cysts after DBS can occur at different locations and at varying postoperative time points. They may present with diverse clinical manifestations or remain completely asymptomatic. Different putative mechanisms and treatment options have been described; however, the paucity of reported clinical cases makes it difficult to speculate on a primary cause.

papers.title: Interaction Between Exercise Intensity and Sedentary Behavior on VO 2 max Change in Patients with De Novo Parkinson Disease: The Study in Parkinson Disease of Exercise (SPARX) Phase 2 Randomized Clinical Trial.
papers.journal: medRxiv : the preprint server for health sciences
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Parkinson disease (PD) is associated with increased sedentary time and reduced cardiorespiratory fitness, making exercise an important component of disease management. Although exercise improves cardiorespiratory fitness, individuals with PD vary substantially in their response to exercise. Sedentary time may contribute to this variability, yet whether sedentary time modifies the response to intervention and varying exercise intensities within an intervention is unknown. We examined whether sedentary time interacted with 6 months of moderate-intensity or high- intensity aerobic exercise on maximal oxygen consumption (VO₂max) in individuals with PD. METHODS: This secondary analysis used data from the SPARX phase 2 randomized clinical trial including 128 de novo PD patients assigned to high- or moderate-intensity treadmill exercise, or usual care for 6 months. Interactions between randomized group and post-randomization 6-months average sedentary time were assessed for associations with 6-month change in VO 2 RESULTS: The interaction between exercise intensity and sedentary behavior on 6-month change in VO 2 CONCLUSIONS: These hypothesis-generating, preliminary findings suggest that sedentary time may modify the response to exercise among individuals participating in moderate-intensity aerobic exercise. Future adequately powered randomized controlled trials are needed to confirm these findings and determine whether sedentary behavior should be considered when prescribing exercise for individuals with PD.

papers.title: The Gut-Brain Axis and Neurodegenerative Diseases: From Mechanistic Pathways to Therapeutic Interventions.
papers.abstract: As the global population ages, the incidence of neurodegenerative diseases (NDDs) has increased. Neurodegenerative diseases have complex pathogenesis and currently lack fundamental treatment methods. The gut-brain axis (GBA) participates in the pathogenesis of NDDs through bidirectional communication between the gut microbiota and the central nervous system (CNS). This review systematically introduces the pathogenic characteristics of representative NDDs such as Alzheimer's disease (AD), Parkinson's disease (PD), and multiple sclerosis (MS), as well as the association mechanisms between these diseases and GBA. The pathogenic characteristics of NDDs are closely related to changes in the composition of the gut microbiota and differences in gut microbiota metabolites (such as short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), neurotransmitters, tryptophan metabolites, etc.). These changes influence the CNS through multiple pathways, including neuroendocrine, vagus nerve, and immune regulation, ultimately contributing to the onset and progression of the diseases. Furthermore, we have collected and summarized preclinical and clinical evidence from recent years regarding therapeutic interventions based on the GBA mechanism, including probiotics, prebiotics, and fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT). Nevertheless, major knowledge gaps remain, particularly regarding causality between gut microbiota changes and NDDs, the underlying molecular mechanisms, and the clinical efficacy of GBA-targeted therapies. This article aims to review the mechanisms of the interaction between the gut microbiota and the brain in neurodegenerative diseases, and based on the existing experimental evidence, provide theoretical basis and future development directions for future prevention and treatment strategies targeting GBA.

papers.title: MIND Diet Adherence and Parkinson's Disease Risk, Progression, and Age at Onset: A Systematic Review.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: The Mediterranean-DASH Intervention for Neurodegenerative Delay (MIND) diet has been associated with cognitive benefits, but its relationship with Parkinson's disease (PD) remains unclear. We systematically reviewed evidence on associations between MIND diet adherence and PD-related outcomes. METHODS: PubMed, Embase, and Google Scholar were searched through June 2026. Eligible observational and interventional studies evaluated MIND diet adherence in relation to PD risk, incident parkinsonism, disease progression, severity, or age at onset. Study quality was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. In case of substantial heterogeneity, findings were synthesized qualitatively. PROSPERO: CRD420251123365. RESULTS: Five observational studies (73,790 participants) were included. Higher MIND diet adherence was associated with lower incident parkinsonism (HR 0.89, 95% CI 0.83-0.96), slower progression of parkinsonian signs, lower PD incidence (HR 0.75, 95% CI 0.58-0.97), and later PD onset. One study found no association with PD risk or progression, whereas another reported lower patient-reported symptom burden with greater MIND diet adherence. Three studies were rated poor quality and one good quality. Certainty of evidence was low for PD incidence and very low for all other outcomes. Quantitative synthesis was not performed because of heterogeneity in outcomes, designs, and effect measures. CONCLUSIONS: Evidence linking MIND diet adherence to PD is limited and observational. Higher adherence may be associated with lower incident parkinsonism, slower progression, reduced PD incidence in selected women, and later PD onset. However, certainty of evidence was low to very low, precluding causal inference. Prospective cohorts and randomized dietary trials are needed.

papers.title: Assistive devices identified as most useful for people with Parkinson's disease - a patient-centered survey.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to identify everyday assistive devices perceived as most useful by people with Parkinson's disease (PwP) and their caregivers. METHODS: A 45-item web-based survey was distributed through the Parkinson & Movement Disorder Alliance website and an online educational event. The survey included four respondent-characteristic items, ratings of 40 assistive devices using a 5-point Likert scale ranging from "not useful" to "very useful," and one free-response item. RESULTS: A total of 293 online surveys were completed. The five devices with the highest percentages of "very useful" ratings were grab bars for shower (80%), grab bars (71%), electric toothbrushes (63%), jar openers (54%), and grabber tools (43%). CONCLUSIONS: Numerous assistive devices are available to make activities of daily living easier for PwP. Identifying which devices PwP and caregivers perceive as most useful may help clinicians prioritize practical recommendations and support greater independence in daily activities.

papers.title: High frequency transcranial pulsed current stimulation improves quality of life in Parkinson's disease: A randomized controlled trial.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive multisystem disorder in which motor and non-motor symptoms impair quality-of-life. High-frequency transcranial pulsed current stimulation (tPCS) modulates network-level dysfunction and may serve as an adjunct therapy in PD. In a randomized controlled trial, 38 participants with Hoehn & Yahr stage I-III PD were randomized to active 400 Hz tPCS or sham for 4 weeks while receiving stable antiparkinsonian medication. Stimulation targeted bilateral dorsolateral prefrontal cortices and motor-cerebellar circuit. Primary outcome was the Parkinson's Disease Questionnaire-39 Summary Index (PDQ-39 SI); secondary outcomes included motor and non-motor measures. Thirty participants completed the study with no serious adverse events. Compared with sham, active tPCS significantly improved PDQ-39 SI (p = 0.017; partial η² = 0.19) and reduced non-motor symptom burden (NMSS, p = 0.005). High frequency tPCS was safe, well tolerated, and improved quality of life in PD, warranting investigation in larger trials. Trial Registration

papers.title: TMEM106B analysis in diverse cohorts suggests no association with Parkinson's disease risk.
papers.journal: medRxiv : the preprint server for health sciences
papers.abstract: Recent evidence suggests that TMEM106B expression is reduced in the brains of patients with Parkinson's disease (PD). However, an association between rare genetic variants in TMEM106B and PD risk has not been previously established. In this work, we investigated the association between rare TMEM106B variants and PD risk. We leveraged whole-genome sequencing data from 22,010 cases and 40,550 controls across diverse ancestries from the Global Parkinson's Genetics Program (GP2), the Accelerating Medicines Partnership in Parkinson's Disease (AMP-PD), and the UK Biobank (UKBB). A total of 4,581 unique rare variants were identified across all groups. We found no evidence that rare coding variants in TMEM106B were associated with PD risk, either individually or through cumulative burden. These findings suggest that rare variation in TMEM106B does not play a major role in PD susceptibility across the populations studied.
